title: Ousted Board Files Emergency Motion to Block Trump’s Name From Being Carved Into Peace Institute
snippet: Former leaders of the U.S. Institute of Peace have asked a federal court to urgently stop contractors from permanently chiseling President Donald Trump’s name onto the nonpartisan agency's headquarters.
content:
WASHINGTON — Ousted board members of the U.S. Institute of Peace filed an emergency motion in federal court Thursday in a bid to stop contractors from permanently carving President Donald Trump’s name into the facade of the organization's Washington, D.C., headquarters.

The urgent legal action comes as the nonpartisan institution remains locked in an ongoing battle with the White House, which previously sought to shutter the peace research center as part of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) initiative.

Battle Over Institutional Identity

According to the filing, DOGE official Kenneth Jackson, who is currently serving as USIP's acting president, has already selected a contractor to chisel Trump's name into the stone exterior on Constitution Avenue. A temporary, bolted-on plaque bearing the president's name was added to the building last December, but former leaders argue that a permanent alteration causes lasting damage.

“The building — which was largely funded by private donations to USIP as a tax-exempt nonprofit corporation — is a work of expressive architecture designed to be ‘symbolic of USIP’s’ independent ‘mission,’” the emergency motion stated. “Alteration of the design to impose a different message would cause irreparable harm.”

Echoes of the Kennedy Center Clash

The dispute closely mirrors recent legal drama surrounding the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, where courts similarly blocked efforts to attach the president’s name to the national landmark. Following that ruling, Trump announced plans to close the performing arts venue and was spotted reviewing plans labeled “Kennedy Center DEMOLISH.”

USIP was originally established under President Ronald Reagan in 1984 to promote global democracy and conflict resolution. While a federal judge ruled in May 2025 that the administration's attempt to dismantle the nonprofit was unlawful, an appeals court panel placed that ruling on hold pending further review.

Attorneys for the ousted board stressed that halting the stone carving would preserve the status quo without harming the administration while the broader court fight over USIP's independence plays out.
